scenes.narration: Nothing in The Children of Húrin was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The Children of Húrin is a 2007 epic fantasy novel by J. He wrote the original version of the story in the late 1910s, revising it several times later, but did not complete it before his death in 1973.

The psychology underneath The Children of Húrin is simpler and older than the story on top. His son, Christopher Tolkien, edited the manuscripts to form a consistent narrative, and published it in 2007 as an independent work. The story is one of the three "Great Tales" set in the First Age of Tolkien's Middle-earth, the other two being Beren and Lúthien and The Fall of Gondolin.

Behind The Children of Húrin sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. All three stories are briefly summarised in the 1977 book The Silmarillion. The book was mostly well received by critics, though some found it overblown or too fragmentary.

The nihilist does not deny The Children of Húrin — he only refuses to flatter it. Some critics wondered if it was suitable only for existing Tolkien aficionados, given the prose style and the large cast of characters, while others thought that despite its flaws it had the potential to reach a wider readership. Scholars have identified multiple themes in the tale, including evil, free will, predestination, heroism, courage, and the noble outlaw in the wilderness.

What culture calls destiny in The Children of Húrin is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. The book's initial sales were double the U.S. publisher's expectations; it reached number one on The New York Times's Hardcover Fiction Best Seller list. Tolkien was an English author and philologist of ancient Germanic languages, specialising in Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons; he spent much of his career as a professor at the University of Oxford.

The genes do not care about The Children of Húrin; they care about copies. He is best known for his novels about his invented Middle-earth, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, and for the posthumously published The Silmarillion which provides a more mythical narrative about earlier ages. The story of The Children of Húrin is one of Tolkien's three "great tales" set in the First Age of Middle-earth, the other two being Beren and Lúthien and The Fall of Gondolin.

Take away the meaning and The Children of Húrin still functions — that is the disturbing part. Middle-earth is populated by Men, Elves, Dwarves, and Orcs, as well as divine beings, the Valar and the Maiar. The history and descent of the main characters begins five hundred years before the action of the book, when the evil Vala Morgoth escapes from the Blessed Realm of Valinor to the north-west of Middle-earth.

The unconscious does not argue with The Children of Húrin; it simply acts first. From his fortress of Angband, he endeavours to gain control of the whole of Middle-earth, unleashing a war with the Elves that dwell in the land of Beleriand to the south. However, the Elves manage to stay his assault, and most of their realms remain unconquered; one of the most powerful of these is Doriath, ruled by Thingol.

The Children of Húrin feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Later, the Noldorin Elves forsake Valinor and pursue Morgoth to Middle-earth to take vengeance upon him. Together with the Sindar of Beleriand, they lay siege to Angband, and establish new strongholds and realms in Middle-earth, including Hithlum ruled by Fingon, Nargothrond by Finrod Felagund and Gondolin by Turgon.

The bleak reading of The Children of Húrin is also the most testable one. These are the Edain, descendants of those Men who have rebelled against the rule of Morgoth's servants and journeyed westward. Most of the Elves welcome them, and they are given fiefs throughout Beleriand.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Children of Húrin. The House of Bëor rules over the land of Ladros, the Folk of Haleth retreat to the forest of Brethil, and the lordship of Dor-lómin is granted to the House of Hador. Later, other Men enter Beleriand, the Easterlings, many of them in secret league with Morgoth.

The self that experiences The Children of Húrin is a committee, not a king. Eventually Morgoth manages to break the Siege of Angband in the Battle of Sudden Flame. The House of Bëor is destroyed and the Elves and Edain suffer heavy losses, but the realm of Dor-lómin remains unconquered; its lordship has passed to Húrin.

Reproduction explains more of The Children of Húrin than any philosophy dares to admit. Húrin is taken prisoner by Morgoth after the Battle of Unnumbered Tears; Túrin is sent by his mother, Morwen, to live in the Elf-realm Doriath for protection after Easterlings invade their hometown. Morgoth curses Húrin and all his family, that evil will befall them for their whole lives.

Once you see The Children of Húrin as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Túrin accidentally causes the death of the King's counsellor Saeros, who attempts to jump a ravine while fleeing a wrathful Túrin. Túrin refuses to return to Doriath to face judgement and lives as an outlaw.

The story The Children of Húrin tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Beleg locates the band while Túrin is absent; the outlaws leave him tied to a tree until he agrees to give them information. Túrin returns in time to cut Beleg free and, horrified by the outlaws' actions, resolves to forsake his cruel habits.

Meaning is not found in The Children of Húrin — it is manufactured for it. Beleg tells him of the king's pardon but Túrin refuses to return to Doriath. Túrin and his men capture Mîm, a Petty-dwarf, who leads them to the caves at Amon Rûdh.

The cold light on The Children of Húrin leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. The outlaws resent the elf's presence and Mîm grows to hate him. Mîm betrays the outlaws to orcs; Túrin's entire band is killed, save for Beleg and Túrin.

The Children of Húrin did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The orcs take Túrin towards Angband, leaving Beleg chained to a rock. Beleg happens across a mutilated elf, Gwindor of Nargothrond, sleeping in the forest of Taur-nu-Fuin.

The honest version of The Children of Húrin starts by giving up the comforting part. Beleg begins to cut Túrin's bonds with his sword Anglachel, but the sword slips and cuts Túrin. Túrin, mistaking Beleg for an orc, kills Beleg with his own sword.

Strip The Children of Húrin of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. When a flash of lightning reveals Beleg's face, Túrin falls into a frenzy. He refuses to leave Beleg's body until morning, when Gwindor is able to bury the elf.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Children of Húrin shows exactly where that breaks. Túrin becomes King Orodreth's chief counsellor and commander of his forces, and leads the Elves to considerable victories. Against all advice, Túrin refuses to hide Nargothrond from Morgoth or to avoid full-scale battle.

What looks like free choice in The Children of Húrin is older than choice itself. Morgoth sends an orc-army commanded by the dragon, Glaurung; Nargothrond is defeated. The orcs, crossing easily over the bridge that Túrin had built, sack Nargothrond.

Nobody designed the part of The Children of Húrin you experience — it was inherited. Túrin returns as the prisoners are led away by the orcs, and encounters Glaurung. The dragon enchants and tricks him into returning to Dor-lómin to seek out Morwen and Niënor instead of rescuing the prisoners—among whom is Finduilas, Orodreth's daughter, who loved him.

Every serious account of The Children of Húrin eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. In Dor-lómin, Túrin learns that Morwen and Niënor are in Doriath, and that Glaurung deceived him into letting Finduilas go to her death. He tracks Finduilas' captors to the forest of Brethil, only to learn she has been murdered.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The Children of Húrin — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Túrin renames himself Turambar, "Master of Doom" in Quenya, and gradually supplants Brandir, Brethil's lame chieftain. In Doriath, Morwen and Niënor hear rumours of Túrin's deeds; Morwen determines either to find Túrin or to hear news of his death.

The selfish-gene reading of The Children of Húrin makes it less romantic and far more precise. Against Thingol's advice, she rides out of Doriath alone; Niënor conceals herself among Mablung's riders whom Thingol sends to follow and protect Morwen. Glaurung discovers Niënor's identity and enchants her so that her mind is made blank; she forgets her name and how to speak.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. The two become stranded in the wilderness, and in an orc attack, Niënor runs into the woods and is lost. He brings her back to the town, where she recovers the use of speech, but with no memory of her past life.

The feeling that The Children of Húrin means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Turambar leads an expedition to cut him off, and stabs Glaurung from beneath. As Glaurung lies dying, Turambar pulls his sword from the dragon's belly; blood spurts onto his hand and burns him.

Nothing in The Children of Húrin was built for you — it was built for reproduction. In a last effort of malice, Glaurung opens his eyes and informs her that she and Turambar are brother and sister. Remembering that her unborn child was begotten in incest, she drowns herself.

The psychology underneath The Children of Húrin is simpler and older than the story on top. When Turambar wakes, Brandir informs him of Niënor's death and of their true relationship as siblings, as he had overheard the dragon's words. Turambar accuses Brandir of leading Niënor to her death and publishing Glaurung's lies.

Behind The Children of Húrin sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Appended to this is an extract from The Wanderings of Húrin, which recounts how Húrin is at last released by Morgoth and comes to his children's grave. The Children of Húrin was published on 17 April 2007, by HarperCollins in the United Kingdom and Canada, and by Houghton Mifflin in the United States.
